text: You get an array of CPU tasks, each labeled with a letter from A to Z, and a number n. In each CPU interval, the CPU can be idle or finish one task. Tasks can run in any order, but two tasks with the same label need a gap of at least n intervals between them. Return the minimum number of intervals to finish all tasks.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the answer counts idle slots too, right? So it's the total length of the schedule, not just the number of tasks. And a gap of n means that after I run an A, the next n slots can't be A.
Yes. Idle slots count. The gap is at least n slots between two same tasks.

Good. One more thing I notice. The labels don't matter, only how many times each label shows up, so I can turn the input into twenty-six counts and forget the letters. Also, idle only matters in the middle — I should never add idle slots at the very end, after the last task. Are there any constraints on the input size?
There are up to ten to the fourth tasks, and each task is an uppercase letter. n is between zero and one hundred.

OK. At most twenty-six different labels, and n can be zero, which means no gap at all. I'll keep that case in mind. Let me run through the examples. Example one: three A's and three B's, with n equal to two. I can do A, B, idle, A, B, idle, A, B. That's eight — note there's no idle at the end. Example two: A, C, A, B, D, B, with n equal to one. There are enough different tasks to fill every gap, so it's just the length, six. Example three: same tasks as example one, but n equal to three. A, B, idle, idle, twice, then A, B. That's ten.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to try every order of the tasks and pick the shortest schedule. That's factorial time — with up to ten thousand tasks, it's hopeless. This problem reminds me of greedy scheduling with a max-heap. The task with the most copies left is the one that can cause idle time, so at each step I run the task with the largest count that is allowed to run. I'll do it in rounds. One round is n plus one slots, and inside a round every task runs at most once. So after a round, every task I used has cooled down, and I can put them all back.

Here's the plan. One: count the letters and push only the non-zero counts into a max-heap. Two: each round, for n plus one slots, pop the biggest count, run it, and park what's left in a small buffer; every slot adds one to time, task or idle. Three: when the round ends, push the buffer back. One thing worth flagging — the stop check needs two conditions. If the heap is empty but the buffer isn't, tasks are still cooling, so the slot is a real idle. If both are empty, I stop and don't pad the round. Checking only the heap turns C, C with n equal to one into two instead of three. And the buffer matters: pushing a task back right away lets it run back-to-back. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I count each letter, push only the non-zero counts into a max-heap, and each pass of the while loop is one round of n plus one slots. Time goes up for both a task slot and an idle slot, and the buffer only goes back after the round. One thing worth flagging — the if f check is not just a speed-up. If I pushed the zeros too, every zero would burn a real slot, and example one would give thirty. Same for cycle equal to n plus one: with cycle equal to n, n equal to zero becomes a round of zero slots, and the loop never ends.

Let's dry-run the code with example one: three A's, three B's, n equal to two, so a cycle of three — expected eight. Rounds one and two each run two tasks, then an idle, because the heap is empty while the buffer still holds cooling tasks. The key moment is round three: after two slots, both the heap and the buffer are empty, so the loop breaks with no idle at the end. Eight, not nine. That matches. Corner cases: a single C with n equal to one returns one. C, C with n equal to one returns three. n equal to zero never idles. Ten thousand A's with n equal to one hundred gives one million nine thousand nine hundred, which fits in an int. And one scary row in the table: a min-heap passes all three examples but fails fifty-four small cases.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is the length plus the answer: each slot does at most one heap operation, and the heap never has more than twenty-six items, so each is constant time. The space complexity is constant — the counts, the heap and the buffer, at most twenty-six each. In the worst-case scenario, the answer is about the max count times n plus one. For ten thousand A's with n equal to one hundred, that's one million nine thousand nine hundred slots, and it still runs in about zero point six to two point four milliseconds.
Can you compute it without simulating?

Yes. There's a formula: the max of the length, and max count minus one, times n plus one, plus the number of labels that share the max count. The most frequent task needs max count minus one full frames, each n plus one slots wide. Then one last row holds only the tasks that also have the max count. For example one, that's two frames of three, plus two, so eight — same as the simulation. Why the max with the length? If other tasks overflow the frames, I just widen them, there's no idle at all, and the answer is the number of tasks — like example two, where the frames give four but the length is six. It's linear with no heap, and it matched the simulation on two hundred thousand random tests. Oh, one more thing — the simulation can still print the actual order.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why the stop check needs both the heap and the buffer empty: idle while tasks cool down counts, but idle at the end doesn't. You showed that a min-heap passes all three examples and still fails, so the max-count-first choice is what makes the greedy correct. And when I asked for no simulation, you gave the frame formula and explained why it's a max with the length. Good work.
